level_platter.title: Level the platter
level_platter.why: A turntable that is not level pulls the arm to one side and loads one groove wall more than the other. It shows up as unequal crosstalk and a lopsided anti-skating result.
level_platter.s1: Put a small, flat spirit level (a round bubble level is ideal) on the platter, next to the spindle.
level_platter.s2: Level it front to back and left to right with the turntable's feet, or with shims under the stand if the feet cannot be adjusted.
level_platter.s3: Turn the platter a quarter turn and check again. A platter that is level in every position also runs true on its bearing.
level_platter.s4: Check the stand as well: it must not rock, and it should not stand right next to a speaker.
level_platter.check: There is no band for this. Crosstalk that stays lopsided whatever you do at the azimuth often comes from a turntable that is not level.
overhang.title: Overhang and zenith (protractor)
overhang.why: The stylus must sit at the right distance from the arm's pivot and point along the groove at two places on the side, the null points. This keeps tracking distortion low across the whole side.
overhang.s1: Print a protractor for your arm: most arm makers offer one, or use a two-point protractor for your arm's pivot-to-spindle distance (Baerwald or Löfgren A are common). Check the printed scale with a ruler.
overhang.s2: Put the protractor on the spindle, lower the stylus onto the inner null point and slide the cartridge in the headshell slots until the stylus sits exactly on the point.
overhang.s3: Turn the cartridge in the headshell until the cantilever, not the cartridge body, runs parallel to the grid lines. Do the same at the outer null point, and go back and forth until both fit.
overhang.s4: Tighten the screws evenly without twisting the cartridge, and check both points once more.
overhang.check: vinyl-check does not measure this directly. Do it once before the first measurement and after every cartridge change.
tracking_force.title: Tracking force
tracking_force.why: With too little force the stylus loses contact on loud passages: it mistracks, distorts and wears the groove. Too much force dulls the sound and wears the stylus faster.
tracking_force.s1: Set anti-skating to zero, remove the stylus guard and balance the arm with the counterweight until it floats level on its own.
tracking_force.s2: Turn only the scale ring of the counterweight to zero, then turn the whole weight to the force the cartridge maker recommends. Start in the upper half of the range.
tracking_force.s3: Check with a stylus force gauge whose platform sits at the height of a record. The scales on counterweights are often off by 0.1–0.3 g.
tracking_force.s4: Set anti-skating back to a starting value (often the same number as the force) and record the side with the anti-skating ramp again.
tracking_force.check: On the anti-skating ramp both channels should stay clean to the end (tracking headroom +11 dB or more). If both break up early, raise the force in steps of 0.1 g within the maker's range.
antiskating.title: Anti-skating
antiskating.why: A spinning record pulls the stylus towards the centre. Anti-skating counters that pull so that both groove walls carry the same load. With too much or too little, one channel distorts first on loud passages.
antiskating.s1: Start with the value the arm maker recommends. On many arms the anti-skating number equals the tracking force.
antiskating.s2: Play the anti-skating ramp (on the AAPT 1: side 2, band 1) with the live measurement open. It shows the distortion of both channels while the level rises.
antiskating.s3: If the left channel distorts first, there is too much anti-skating: turn it down a little. If the right channel distorts first, there is too little: turn it up.
antiskating.s4: Change it in small steps and play the ramp after each step, until both channels break up at the same level or both stay clean to the end.
antiskating.check: Record the side with the ramp again: the anti-skating finding should read ok, or balanced with a high tracking headroom.
vta.title: Arm height (VTA)
vta.why: The arm height sets the angle at which the stylus stands in the groove. A wrong angle raises distortion, above all intermodulation, and tilts the treble.
vta.s1: Start with the arm parallel to the record, seen from the side, with the mat and record you normally use on the platter.
vta.s2: Note the current height. Change it in small steps (about 1 mm at the pivot), one step per alignment run.
vta.s3: After each step, record the side with the intermodulation band (on the AAPT 1: side 1) and compare the runs.
vta.s4: Keep the height with the lowest intermodulation and mark it on the arm.
vta.check: Target: intermodulation 3 % or less. If the value hardly changes, the arm height is not critical with this cartridge: leave the arm parallel.
azimuth.title: Azimuth (cartridge tilt)
azimuth.why: Seen from the front, the stylus must stand upright in the groove. A tilted cartridge lets more of one channel leak into the other than the other way round.
azimuth.s1: Seen from the front, check that the cartridge sits straight in the headshell. A small mirror on the platter helps.
azimuth.s2: If the arm allows it (azimuth screw, rotating headshell or arm tube), loosen the adjustment and turn it by a very small amount.
azimuth.s3: Record the side with the crosstalk bands (left only, right only) again. If the difference between the two directions grew, turn the other way.
azimuth.s4: Repeat until the crosstalk is about the same in both directions. Arms without an azimuth adjustment can be corrected with a thin shim between cartridge and headshell on one side.
azimuth.check: Target: both crosstalk values within 3 dB of each other, each −25 dB or better for a good MM cartridge (see its data sheet).
input_level.title: Recording level
input_level.why: The level must leave room for loud records without clipping and stay well above the noise of the converter. vinyl-check counts pops relative to the reference tone.
input_level.s1: Play the 1 kHz reference tone (on the AAPT 1: side 1, band 1) and open Check level.
input_level.s2: Set the gain of the interface or phono stage so that the tone reads about −20 dBFS on both channels.
input_level.s3: Mark the setting and leave it alone from then on. Note it in the alignment run.
input_level.s4: A USB turntable with a fixed level cannot be changed: tick “Level not adjustable on the device” in its profile.
input_level.check: Target: −24 to −16 dBFS. Record the side with the reference tone again.
speed.title: Speed
speed.why: A wrong speed changes pitch and tempo, and the skip detection looks for the true revolution time.
speed.s1: Let the turntable run for a few minutes first: belts and motors settle once warm.
speed.s2: Direct drive: set the pitch control to zero or switch on the quartz lock. Belt drive: clean the belt, the pulley and the platter rim with a lint-free cloth, and replace a shiny or stretched belt.
speed.s3: If the turntable has speed trimmers (small potentiometers, often under the platter or the base), turn them in small steps as the maker's manual describes.
speed.s4: Record the side with the 3150 Hz band again.
speed.check: Target: within ±0.5 %. vinyl-check allows for small deviations in the skip detection, but you hear them.
wow_flutter.title: Wow & flutter
wow_flutter.why: An unsteady speed makes long tones waver. It comes from the drive (belt, motor, idler wheel), the bearing, or a record that is not centred.
wow_flutter.s1: Check that the test record sits centred. An off-centre hole alone causes measurable wow.
wow_flutter.s2: Belt drive: clean or replace the belt and check that it runs in the middle of the pulley. Idler drive: clean the idler wheel.
wow_flutter.s3: Check the main bearing: it should turn freely and quietly. Oil it as the maker specifies.
wow_flutter.s4: Record the side with the 3150 Hz band again.
balance.title: Channel balance
balance.why: Both channels should play the same tone equally loud. A difference shifts the stereo image and every comparison between the channels.
balance.s1: Check the azimuth first: a tilted cartridge changes the balance too.
balance.s2: Check the cartridge pins and headshell leads: firm, clean contacts, each colour on its pin.
balance.s3: Check that the channel controls of the interface or phono stage are set alike. Swap the left and right cables: if the difference moves with the cable, it is not the cartridge.
balance.s4: Cartridges have a balance tolerance (often 1–2 dB, see the data sheet). A difference within it is normal.
balance.check: Target: within ±1 dB. Record the side with the reference tone again.
resonance.title: Arm/cartridge resonance
resonance.why: The effective mass of the arm and the compliance of the cartridge form a spring. Its resonance should lie between 8 and 12 Hz: lower, record warps excite it; higher, it reaches into the bass.
resonance.s1: This is a question of matching arm and cartridge, not a setting. Look up the effective mass of the arm and the compliance of the cartridge (at 10 Hz).
resonance.s2: Resonance too high: add mass at the headshell (a heavier headshell or a small weight). Resonance too low: a lighter headshell, or a cartridge with lower compliance.
resonance.s3: Some arms have a damping trough or exchangeable counterweights; these shift and damp the resonance too.
resonance.s4: Record the side with the vertical bass sweep again.
resonance.check: Target: 8–12 Hz. Between 7 and 15 Hz is usually fine for playing records.
loading.title: Treble (cartridge loading)
loading.why: With moving-magnet cartridges the treble depends on the load: the input resistance and capacitance of the phono stage plus the cable.
loading.s1: Look up the load the cartridge maker recommends: usually 47 kΩ and a range of capacitance in pF.
loading.s2: Set the phono stage or interface to it if it can be switched, and count the capacitance of the cable (often 100–200 pF) as part of it.
loading.s3: Raised treble often means too much capacitance. Falling treble can also mean a worn stylus or a wrong arm height.
loading.s4: Record the side with the frequency sweep again.
loading.check: Target: within ±2 dB up to 10 kHz. Moving-coil cartridges hardly react to the load.
phono_eq.title: Bass and RIAA equalization
phono_eq.why: Records are cut with the bass lowered and the treble raised (RIAA); the phono stage reverses it. A deviation at 100 Hz or in the bass sweep points to the phono stage, not to the turntable.
phono_eq.s1: Compare the channels: if only one deviates, check its cable and contacts.
phono_eq.s2: If the phono stage has a subsonic or rumble filter, keep in mind that it lowers the deepest bass on purpose.
phono_eq.s3: Another phono stage or input shows whether the deviation goes with it.
phono_eq.s4: Deviations up to 1–2 dB are normal and do not change what the record check counts.
phono_eq.check: Target: 100 Hz against 1 kHz within ±1 dB. Record the side with the 100 Hz band again.
rumble.title: Rumble and hum
rumble.why: Low-frequency noise comes from the motor, the bearing or the place the turntable stands on; hum comes from grounding and cables.
rumble.s1: Connect the turntable's ground lead to the phono stage or interface. Keep signal cables away from mains cables and power supplies.
rumble.s2: Put the turntable on a rigid, stable surface away from the speakers. A wall shelf helps on floors that move when you walk.
rumble.s3: Check bearing and motor: a dry bearing or a worn motor mount adds rumble.
rumble.s4: Record the side with the silent groove again.
rumble.check: Target: −55 dB or lower against the reference. The spectrum shows whether the lines sit at 50/60 Hz (hum) or lower (mechanics).
stylus_care.title: Stylus and test record
stylus_care.why: Clicks in the silent groove of the test record come from the chain itself: dust on the stylus, static, or a worn test record. vinyl-check subtracts this floor from every record.
stylus_care.s1: Clean the stylus with a soft brush from back to front, never sideways.
stylus_care.s2: Keep the test record clean and free of static, and store it in an anti-static sleeve.
stylus_care.s3: Keep track of the stylus hours: a worn stylus raises the click floor and the distortion.
stylus_care.s4: Record the side with the silent groove again after cleaning.
stylus_care.check: The click floor should be low and about the same from run to run. A rising floor means the stylus or the test record needs care.
